openingProblem.problem: In 1945 the Communist parties of eastern Europe were tiny. By 1949 they ruled every state between the Baltic and the Adriatic. Did they win power, take it, or receive it from Moscow?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: how did the Communists come to rule eastern Europe?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Why did Stalin want control of eastern Europe?
chunks.body:
Stalin explained his thinking to the Yugoslav Communist Milovan Djilas before the war ended: "whoever occupies a territory also imposes upon it his own social system. Everyone imposes his own system as far as his army can reach." Tony Judt argues that this was the core of Soviet policy. The war had been fought to defeat Germany and restore Russian security in the west. Between Germany and Russia lay a belt of small, vulnerable states, from Finland to Yugoslavia, whose governments between the wars had, with the partial exception of Czechoslovakia, been hostile to Moscow. The only acceptable outcome for Stalin was governments that could never threaten Soviet security.

Judt's point is that security and Communism were not alternatives. The only way to guarantee friendly governments was to make their political systems like the Soviet one, and "this, from the start, was what Stalin wanted and intended". Coalition governments in 1945 did not mean that Stalin was undecided. They were a route to power for parties that were weak.

The method was shaped by the Red Army. Soviet troops stayed in Hungary until the mid-1950s, in Romania until 1958, and in East Germany for the whole of its life. Moscow could also present itself as a protector: Poland and Czechoslovakia had expelled their Germans, and many people feared a German revival. Judt adds that democracy had shallow roots in the region. Its inter-war regimes had been corrupt and authoritarian, and the real governing class had been the bureaucracy, so the move to Communist "popular democracy" was "a short move and an easy one".

Once in power, Stalin secured loyalty in the only way he knew: a party monopoly. The Hungarian constitution of August 1949 gave the party a "leading role"; the party became the sole route to promotion and, through its control of the courts, the dispenser of justice. This mattered because Soviet control did not depend on popularity, which meant that once the party owned the state, elections and public opinion no longer decided who ruled.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Stalin's main motive was security: a buffer of reliable states between Germany and the USSR.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Judt argues security and Communism were the same aim, since only Communist governments could be relied on.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Red Army made control possible, wherever local Communists were weak.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In Czechoslovakia the Red Army left in 1945 and the Communists still took power, so force was not the only route.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Weak democratic traditions made the takeover easier.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Where elections were free, Communists lost them, which shows popular resistance was real.

howItGetsAsked: Discuss the view that Stalin's main aim in eastern Europe after 1945 was security, not the spread of Communism.
To what extent was Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1945 and 1955 based on force?

useItInAnEssay.claim: Stalin's control of eastern Europe served security first, but he saw Communism as the only way to secure it.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Judt argues that the only acceptable outcome for Stalin was governments that could never threaten Soviet security, and that aligning their political systems with the USSR's was what he intended from the start.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the spread of Communism was the means of achieving security, so the two aims cannot be separated.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Stalin tolerated independent farmers and the Catholic Church in Poland for the sake of stability, which suggests security mattered more than ideological uniformity.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Security was therefore the end and Communism the method, which is why control was imposed so thoroughly.

chunks.title: How the Communists took power, 1945–1948
chunks.body:
In 1945 the Communist parties of eastern Europe were tiny. Mátyás Rákosi returned to Budapest in February 1945 with perhaps 4,000 Communists behind him; the Romanian party had fewer than 1,000 members in a country of nearly 20 million. Only in the industrial Czech lands and in Yugoslavia, where Communists had led the resistance, was there a mass base.

Stalin therefore began with **"Front" coalitions** of Communists, Socialists and other anti-Fascist parties. The East German Communist leader Walter Ulbricht explained the tactic privately in 1945: "It's quite clear—it's got to look democratic, but we must have everything in our control." Communists rarely asked to be president or prime minister. Instead they took the Ministry of the Interior, which controlled the police and newspaper licences; the Ministry of Justice, which ran purges and courts; and the Ministry of Agriculture, which distributed land to millions of peasants.

Elections soon showed that the ballot box would not bring them to power. In November 1945 the Smallholders won an absolute majority in Hungary. In Poland the Peasant Party of Stanisław Mikołajczyk had about 600,000 members in December 1945, ten times the Communists' activists. So the parties turned to **pressure and terror**. In 1946 and 1947 opponents were smeared, beaten, arrested and tried as "Fascists". In Bulgaria the Agrarian leader Nikola Petkov was arrested the day after the US Senate ratified the peace treaties in June 1947, and executed within 96 hours of American recognition of the government that September. Rigged elections followed: in Poland in January 1947 the Communist-led bloc was credited with 80 per cent; in Hungary in August 1947, even with Rajk falsifying the count, the Communists won only 22 per cent.

The Socialists were harder to brand as Fascists, so the Communists absorbed them. The Socialist Unity Party was created in the Soviet zone of Germany in 1946, and similar forced mergers followed in 1948 in Romania, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria and Poland. This mattered because the Socialists were the only rivals with working-class support, which meant that their absorption left no organised opposition. By May 1949 Hungary's "People's Front" was credited with 95.6 per cent of the vote.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The takeover was gradual: coalitions, key ministries, then terror and forced mergers.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: In Romania and Bulgaria the Soviet hand was heavy from the start, so the stages were short.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Communists lost free elections, so control depended on coercion, not consent.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Land reform and protection against Germany won Communists some real support.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Western diplomacy shaped the timing: opponents were destroyed once peace treaties were signed.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The pattern was set by Moscow, not by Western actions.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Communists gained power in eastern Europe mainly by capturing the instruments of coercion, not by winning votes.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In every coalition they took the Ministries of the Interior and Justice, and in Hungary even an election falsified by the Communist Interior Minister gave them only 22 per cent in August 1947.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that control of the police and courts let them arrest opponents and rig results, so electoral defeat did not stop them.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, in Czechoslovakia they won 40.2 per cent of the Czech vote in free elections in 1946, so in one state they had real support.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Control of the police was therefore the decisive method, with genuine popularity the exception.

chunks.title: Prague 1948 and the machinery of the bloc
chunks.body:
Czechoslovakia was the exception that ended the exceptions. It had a democratic tradition and a strong Communist Party of its own, and the Red Army had left in November 1945. In the free elections of May 1946 the Communists won 40.2 per cent in the Czech lands. But in February 1948, when non-Communist ministers resigned in protest at Communist infiltration of the police, the party seized full control. Judt calls the **Prague coup** "of enormous significance" because it happened in a friendly, more or less democratic country: it convinced the West that Communism was on the march.

By then Moscow was building institutions to hold the bloc together. In September 1947, at Szklarska Poręba in Poland, Stalin founded the **Cominform**. Its stated aim was coordination; its real aim, Judt argues, was to re-establish Soviet dominion over the Communist movement. Andrei Zhdanov announced that the world was divided into two irreconcilable "camps". In January 1949 came **Comecon**, the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance. Each state traded bilaterally with the USSR and was given a fixed role: East Germany, Czechoslovakia and Hungary supplied industrial goods at prices set by Moscow, Poland and Romania food and raw materials. Judt compares the structure to colonialism. Czechoslovakia, richer than France per head before the war, was by 1956 poorer than it had been twenty years earlier.

Inside each state the Soviet model was copied. By December 1948 the state owned 83 per cent of Hungarian industry and 98 per cent of Bulgarian. From 1949 collectivisation was forced on the peasants, though not in Poland, where Stalin tolerated independent farmers and the Catholic Church for the sake of stability. After 1948 the hunt for "Titoists" produced **show trials**. In Hungary the former Interior Minister László Rajk confessed to being an Anglo-American agent and was hanged in October 1949. In Prague the party's General Secretary, Rudolf Slánský, was tried in November 1952 with thirteen others, most of them Jews; eleven were executed. This mattered because the trials struck at loyal Communists, which meant that no one in the bloc could feel safe from Moscow.

The machinery was completed in May 1955, ten days after West Germany joined NATO, when the USSR announced the **Warsaw Pact**: a military alliance of the satellites under a unified command.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Institutions such as the Cominform and Comecon tied the satellites to Moscow politically and economically.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Cominform met only three times and was disbanded in 1956, so its practical role was limited.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet economic control distorted the satellites' economies.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Heavy industry grew fast at first: steel output in East Germany rose from 120,000 tons to over 2 million tons.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Terror within the parties enforced obedience after 1948.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The trials were aimed at Communists, so they show insecurity in Moscow as much as strength.

howItGetsAsked: Analyse the role of Comecon and the Cominform in Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1947 and 1955.
Compare and contrast the Communist takeovers in Poland and Czechoslovakia between 1945 and 1948.

useItInAnEssay.claim: Comecon tied the satellites to the Soviet Union by making their economies dependent on Moscow.
useItInAnEssay.prove: From January 1949 each state traded bilaterally with the USSR and was assigned a fixed role, supplying industrial goods or food at prices Moscow set.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the satellites could not develop independent trade with the West, so economic dependence reinforced political control.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the system also damaged the satellites: Czechoslovakia was poorer by 1956 than twenty years earlier, which stored up resentment.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Comecon therefore strengthened Soviet control in the short term while weakening the economies that control depended on.

chunks.title: Tito: the limits of Soviet control
chunks.body:
Yugoslavia shows where Soviet control stopped. Tito's Communists were the only party in Europe to come to power by their own efforts, through the partisan war against German and Italian occupation. They were, at first, more radical than Moscow. In the elections of November 1945 voters chose between Tito's People's Front and an urn labelled "opposition"; a constitution copied from the Soviet one followed in January 1946, and 7,000 collective farms were set up before collectivisation had begun elsewhere.

That independence was the problem. Judt explains that Stalin wanted Moscow to be not *a* model of revolution but *the* model. Tito's plan for a Balkan Federation including Albania and Bulgaria looked like a bid for regional power. His support for the Greek Communist insurgents and his claims on Trieste and Carinthia provoked the West at a time when Stalin did not want a quarrel over secondary issues. In February 1948 Stalin condemned the Balkan Federation; Soviet advisers were withdrawn; and on 28 June 1948 the Cominform expelled Yugoslavia for failing to acknowledge the leading role of the USSR. Judt's judgement is that "Stalin needed to break Tito in order to make very clear to Tito's fellow Communists that Moscow would brook no dissent."

Tito was not broken. Yugoslav trade with the Soviet bloc fell from 46 per cent of the total in 1948 to 14 per cent a year later, and the threat of invasion was real, so Tito turned to the West: between 1949 and 1955 Western aid came to $1.2 billion, of which only $55 million was repaid. Yugoslavia then went its own way. By 1951 most economic enterprises had been handed from the federal government to the republics; a decree of March 1953 let peasants leave the collectives, and by 1954 80 per cent of farmland was private again. The party kept its monopoly of power.

Inside the bloc the split had harsh consequences. "Nationalism" became the main enemy; the hunt for "Titoists" produced the show trials, and in Hungary alone some 2,000 Communist cadres were executed. This mattered because Tito proved that a Communist state could survive outside Soviet control, which meant that Stalin tightened control everywhere else to stop the example spreading.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Tito could defy Stalin because his regime did not depend on the Red Army.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Without Western aid he would have struggled to survive the boycott, so his independence depended on the West.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The split was about power and obedience, not ideology: Tito was more radical than Stalin.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The Balkan Federation and Greece were concrete policy disputes, not only questions of loyalty.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The split made Stalin tighten control elsewhere, through purges and show trials.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: The trials also served other aims, such as the antisemitic campaign of 1952–53.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the split between Tito and Stalin in 1948.
To what extent was Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1945 and 1955 based on force?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Tito–Stalin split was caused above all by Stalin's refusal to accept a Communist leader he did not control.
useItInAnEssay.prove: Tito's party had come to power without the Red Army, and his plans for a Balkan Federation and his support for the Greek insurgents ran ahead of Soviet policy.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Tito's success offered other Communists a model independent of Moscow, which, as Judt argues, Stalin had to break to show that Moscow would brook no dissent.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the immediate disputes over Greece, Trieste and the Balkan Federation were real policy conflicts, not only a test of loyalty.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The split was therefore about authority more than ideology, since Tito was if anything more radical than Stalin.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1945 and 1955 based on force?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far control rested on force rather than consent, institutions or ideology

modelPlan.thesis: Soviet control rested largely on force, because Communists lost free elections and relied on the police, terror and the Red Army; but party monopoly and institutions such as Comecon turned force into a lasting system.

arguments.claim: Force: the Red Army, the police and terror against opponents (named factor first).
Elections were lost or rigged, so consent was limited.
Institutions: party monopoly, Cominform, Comecon, Warsaw Pact.
The limit of force: Tito's Yugoslavia.

modelPlan.counter: In Czechoslovakia the Communists won 40.2 per cent of the Czech vote in free elections, and Soviet protection against Germany had real appeal.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without force, would Communists have ruled? Almost nowhere, so force was the foundation, even if institutions made it lasting.

segments.text: Soviet control of eastern Europe was based largely on force, because the Communists could not win power by consent.
In Hungary's August 1947 elections, even with Rajk falsifying the count, the Communists won only 22 per cent, and Poland's 80 per cent in January 1947 was produced by rigging.
This meant that power came from the police and the courts the Communists controlled, backed by the Red Army, so votes did not decide who ruled.
However, in Czechoslovakia the Communists won 40.2 per cent of the Czech vote in free elections in 1946, which shows real support in at least one state.
Force was therefore the foundation of Soviet control, with genuine consent the exception rather than the rule.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “Stalin's main aim in eastern Europe after 1945 was security, not the spread of Communism.” Discuss with reference to the period 1945 to 1953.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The claim that security, not Communism, was the aim
decodeKey.judgement: Which aim mattered more, or whether they were the same

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is largely right that security was Stalin's end, but wrong to separate it from Communism: Stalin believed only Soviet-style governments could guarantee security, so Communism was his method.

arguments.claim: For: the aim of governments that could never threaten the USSR.
For: tolerance of private farms and the Church in Poland for stability.
Against: the systematic imposition of the Soviet model, party monopoly and Comecon.
Against: the break with Tito, a Communist more radical than Stalin.

modelPlan.counter: The break with the most Communist of the satellites shows that obedience, not ideology, was what Stalin demanded.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: What did Stalin refuse to tolerate? Unreliable governments, never non-Communist farming, so security was the end.

segments.text: Stalin's main aim was security, but he believed only Communist governments could provide it.
Judt argues that the only acceptable outcome was governments that could never threaten Soviet security, and that Stalin intended from the start to align their systems with the USSR's.
This meant that spreading Communism was the method of securing the border, so the two aims were in practice one.
However, Stalin tolerated independent farmers and the Church in Poland for stability, which shows he would sacrifice ideological uniformity for security.
The claim is therefore valid about Stalin's end, but misleading if it suggests Communism did not matter to him.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the split between Tito and Stalin in 1948.

decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most serious

modelPlan.thesis: The split was caused mainly by Stalin's refusal to accept a Communist leader he did not control; its main consequence was a tightening of control across the rest of the bloc.

arguments.claim: Cause: Tito's independent power base.
Cause: Balkan Federation, Greece and Trieste.
Consequence: Yugoslavia survived with Western aid and went its own way.
Consequence: purges and show trials of 'Titoists'.

modelPlan.counter: The specific disputes over Greece and Trieste could have caused a split even with a loyal leader.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? The proof that a Communist state could survive outside Soviet control.

segments.text: The split was caused above all by Stalin's refusal to accept a Communist leader he did not control.
Tito's party had come to power by its own efforts, and on 28 June 1948 the Cominform expelled Yugoslavia for failing to acknowledge the leading role of the USSR.
This meant that the charge was disobedience, not insufficient Communism, so the split was about authority.
However, Tito's support for the Greek insurgents and his claims on Trieste were real policy conflicts that endangered Stalin's relations with the West.
The deepest cause was therefore Tito's independence, with the policy disputes as triggers.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast the Communist takeovers in Poland and Czechoslovakia between 1945 and 1948.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: Both takeovers ended in Communist monopoly and both relied on control of the police, but they differed fundamentally: Poland's Communists had little support and needed rigged elections, while Czechoslovakia's had real support and took power by coup.

arguments.claim: Similarity: Communists controlled the police and key ministries.
Similarity: Socialists forcibly absorbed in 1948.
Difference: weak support and rigged elections in Poland.
Difference: real support, no Red Army, then the February coup in Czechoslovakia.

modelPlan.counter: The outcome was the same, so the differences in route may matter less than the common dependence on Moscow.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Popular support, because it explains why Czechoslovakia needed a coup rather than rigged elections.

segments.text: The takeovers in Poland and Czechoslovakia ended alike but began from opposite positions.

In Poland the Peasant Party had ten times the Communists' activists and the Communist bloc's 80 per cent in January 1947 was rigged, whereas in Czechoslovakia the Communists won 40.2 per cent of the Czech vote freely in 1946.
This meant that Polish Communists needed fraud to rule from the start, while Czech Communists, who had expected to win at the ballot box, used a government crisis to seize power in February 1948.
However, in both states control of the police was decisive, and in both the Socialists were absorbed in 1948.
The key difference was therefore the degree of popular support, while the decisive similarity was control of coercion.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the role of Comecon and the Cominform in Soviet control of eastern Europe between 1947 and 1955.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.judgement: How much each institution added to control, compared with force and the parties

modelPlan.thesis: Comecon mattered more than the Cominform: it bound the satellites' economies to Moscow for decades, while the Cominform was mainly a tool for enforcing political discipline in 1947–48 and met only three times.

arguments.claim: The Cominform imposed the 'two camps' line and expelled Tito.
Comecon made each economy dependent on bilateral trade with the USSR.
Copying the Soviet model inside each state: nationalisation and collectivisation.
The Warsaw Pact completed the system militarily.

modelPlan.counter: The decisive instruments were the party monopoly and the Red Army; institutions only formalised control already won.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which institution made control last? Comecon, because dependence outlived the Cominform, which was disbanded in 1956.

segments.text: Comecon did more than the Cominform to entrench Soviet control.
From January 1949 each satellite traded bilaterally with the USSR and was assigned a fixed role, while the Cominform met only three times before being disbanded in 1956.
This meant that economic dependence was built into the structure of every satellite, so control did not depend on meetings or slogans.
However, the Cominform was the instrument that expelled Tito in 1948, which shows its political importance at a decisive moment.
Comecon was therefore the more lasting tool of control, the Cominform the sharper one.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the methods used by Communist parties to gain power in eastern Europe between 1945 and 1948.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.judgement: Which methods were decisive and how they worked together

modelPlan.thesis: The Communists gained power mainly by capturing the instruments of coercion inside coalition governments, then using them to destroy opponents, absorb the Socialists and rig elections.

arguments.claim: Front coalitions as a route to power.
Capturing the Interior, Justice and Agriculture ministries.
Terror, show trials and rigged elections.
Forced mergers with the Socialists, and a coup where needed.

modelPlan.counter: Land reform and fear of Germany gave the Communists some real support, so methods were not only coercive.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without which method would the others have failed? Control of the police, which made terror and rigging possible.

segments.text: The decisive method was the capture of the Ministry of the Interior inside coalition governments.
In every coalition the Communists sought the Interior, which controlled the police and press licences, and the Justice ministry, which ran purges and courts.
This meant they could arrest opponents as 'Fascists' and falsify elections, as Rajk did in Hungary in 1947, so electoral defeat no longer mattered.
However, in Czechoslovakia the Communists also had real popular support, winning 40.2 per cent of the Czech vote in 1946.
Control of the police was therefore the method that made all the others possible.
